Supplementary Code: A rolling-window approach for detecting aggregation behaviour from telemetry data

Case study: tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) at North West Island, southern Great Barrier Reef

Overview

This document reproduces the workflow used to identify aggregation events — occasions when two or more tagged individuals are detected at the same acoustic receiver within a short period of time — from passive acoustic telemetry detection data.

The approach has four stages:

  1. Build a time window around every detection. Each detection is given a window of ± time_window_mins (10 minutes in this case study).
  2. Find co-detections. Two detections are linked when they come from different individuals, at the same receiver, and fall within time_window_mins of each other.
  3. Chain co-detections into events. Linked detections are treated as a network; every connected group of detections (a network “component”) is one aggregation event. An event therefore continues for as long as each detection in it lies within time_window_mins of a detection of another individual at that receiver.
  4. Summarise events. For each event we report its start and end time, duration, the number of individuals involved, how long each individual was present, and the shortest period in which all individuals in the event were detected.

Note that detections of a single individual are never linked to one another directly. A shark that remains at a receiver after the others have left is only part of the event while it is within time_window_mins of a detection of another individual.

Data

The case study uses tiger shark detections from receivers deployed at North West Island (NWI), Capricorn–Bunker Group, in Queensland, Australia. Receivers at NWI were deployed as a VEMCO Positioning System (VPS) array; here, however, each receiver is treated as an independent listening station and aggregations are defined by co-detection at the same receiver (i.e. within that receiver’s detection range), not from estimated VPS positions.

Data were downloaded from the IMOS Australian Animal Acoustic Telemetry Database (https://animaltracking.aodn.org.au/detection) with the filters Species Name = “Tiger Shark” and Installation Name = “IMOS North West Island” The column names are those of the standard IMOS detection export, so the code can be applied to any data downloaded from the same portal.

Setup

Packages

library(data.table)  # fast interval overlap joins (foverlaps) and grouping
library(lubridate)   # time zone conversion
library(dplyr)       # data summaries
library(ggplot2)     # plotting
library(igraph)      # grouping linked detections into events (connected components)

User-defined parameters

All analysis choices are set here so they can be changed in one place.

# Path to the detection file, relative to this .Rmd file
data_file <- "Data/Tigers_NWI.csv"

# Maximum time (minutes) between detections of two different individuals at the
# same receiver for them to be considered together. Choose this with reference to
# the transmitter's nominal ping interval and the behaviour of the study species.
time_window_mins <- 10

# Local time zone of the study site. IMOS detection timestamps are in UTC.
local_tz <- "Australia/Brisbane"

# Number of receivers to keep for the case study: those that detected the greatest
# number of different individuals.
n_focal_stations <- 5

Data preparation

Read in detections

Tigers_NWI <- read.csv(data_file, header = TRUE)

# Detections, individuals and receivers in the raw data
c(detections  = nrow(Tigers_NWI),
  individuals = n_distinct(Tigers_NWI$transmitter_deployment_id),
  receivers   = n_distinct(Tigers_NWI$station_name))
##  detections individuals   receivers 
##      126280          68          24

Number of individuals detected at each receiver

Aggregations can only be detected where several tagged individuals occur, so we first count how many different individuals were detected at each receiver.

unique_counts_NWI <- Tigers_NWI %>%
  group_by(station_name) %>%
  summarise(n_unique = n_distinct(transmitter_deployment_id)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_unique))

unique_counts_NWI

Select focal receivers

To illustrate the method, the analysis is restricted to the receivers that detected the most individuals. With the full NWI dataset these are VPS5_NWI, VPS4_NWI, South 1, VPS7_NWI and Green Zone.

focal_stations <- head(unique_counts_NWI$station_name, n_focal_stations)

Tigers_NWI <- Tigers_NWI %>% filter(station_name %in% focal_stations)

focal_stations
## [1] "VPS5_NWI" "VPS4_NWI" "VPS6_NWI" "VPS7_NWI" "VPS9_NWI"

Convert timestamps from UTC to local time

IMOS timestamps are supplied in UTC. They are converted to local time (AEST, UTC+10; Queensland does not observe daylight saving) so that event times can be interpreted in terms of time of day.

Tigers_NWI$detection_datetime <- as.POSIXct(Tigers_NWI$detection_datetime,
                                            format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC")
Tigers_NWI$detection_datetime <- with_tz(Tigers_NWI$detection_datetime, tzone = local_tz)

Keep required columns and convert to a data.table

Only four columns are needed. transmitter_deployment_id is used to identify individuals because it is unique to each tag deployment, whereas a transmitter_id code can be reused if a tag is redeployed on another animal.

Tigers_NWI <- Tigers_NWI %>%
  dplyr::select(detection_datetime, transmitter_id, transmitter_deployment_id, station_name)

Tigers_NWI_dt <- as.data.table(Tigers_NWI)
setorder(Tigers_NWI_dt, station_name, detection_datetime)

# Unique row identifier for each detection; used as the node ID in the network step
Tigers_NWI_dt[, id := .I]

Identifying aggregation events

Step 1: Create a time window around each detection

Each detection is given a window extending time_window_mins either side of its timestamp.

window_secs <- time_window_mins * 60

Tigers_NWI_dt[, start := detection_datetime - window_secs]
Tigers_NWI_dt[, end   := detection_datetime + window_secs]

Step 2: Find detections that fall within each other’s windows

data.table::foverlaps() joins two tables of intervals and returns every pair that overlaps. Table x holds the window around each detection; table y holds each detection as a zero-length interval (start = end = detection time). An overlap therefore means that detection j occurred within time_window_mins of detection i.

station_name is included as the first key column so detections are only compared with other detections at the same receiver.

x <- Tigers_NWI_dt[, .(station_name, start, end, transmitter_deployment_id, id)]
y <- Tigers_NWI_dt[, .(station_name, start = detection_datetime, end = detection_datetime,
                       transmitter_deployment_id, id)]

setkey(x, station_name, start, end)
setkey(y, station_name, start, end)

dt_overlap <- foverlaps(x, y, nomatch = 0L)

In the output of foverlaps(), columns from x are prefixed with i. (e.g. i.id), and unprefixed columns come from y.

Step 3: Keep only pairs of different individuals

Overlaps between detections of the same individual (including each detection with itself) are discarded. What remains are co-detections: pairs of different individuals detected at the same receiver within time_window_mins of each other.

dt_overlap <- dt_overlap[transmitter_deployment_id != i.transmitter_deployment_id]

nrow(dt_overlap)  # number of co-detection pairs (each pair appears twice, once in each direction)
## [1] 61026

Step 4: Chain co-detections into events

Each detection is a node in a network and each co-detection pair is an edge. igraph::components() finds the connected components of this network: groups of detections linked directly or through a chain of other co-detections. Each component is given an Event_ID.

All detections are added as nodes, so detections with no co-detection form components of size one. These are removed in Step 6, when events with fewer than two individuals are discarded.

edges <- dt_overlap[, .(from = id, to = i.id)]

g <- graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = FALSE,
                           vertices = data.frame(name = Tigers_NWI_dt$id))

membership <- components(g)$membership  # named by node (detection) id

Tigers_NWI_dt[, Event_ID := as.integer(membership[as.character(id)])]

Because edges only join detections at the same receiver, every event belongs to a single receiver.

Step 5: Summarise each event

For each event we record the time of its first and last detection and the number of different individuals detected.

event_summary_NWI <- Tigers_NWI_dt[, .(
  Event_Start_Time = min(detection_datetime),
  Event_End_Time   = max(detection_datetime),
  Max_N_Sharks     = uniqueN(transmitter_deployment_id)),
  by = .(station_name, Event_ID)]

Step 6: Keep events involving two or more individuals

The event summary is joined back to the detection-level data, and components containing a single individual (i.e. detections that were not co-detected with another shark) are removed. The helper columns used for the overlap join are then dropped.

Tigers_NWI_final <- merge(Tigers_NWI_dt, event_summary_NWI,
                          by = c("station_name", "Event_ID"), all.x = TRUE)

Tigers_NWI_final <- Tigers_NWI_final[Max_N_Sharks >= 2]

Tigers_NWI_final[, c("start", "end", "id") := NULL]

# Event-level table restricted to aggregation events
events_NWI <- event_summary_NWI[Max_N_Sharks >= 2]

if (nrow(events_NWI) == 0) {
  message("No aggregation events were found with a ", time_window_mins,
          "-minute window. Results tables and the event plot below will be empty.")
}

Tigers_NWI_final holds one row per detection that belongs to an aggregation event; events_NWI holds one row per event.

Describing aggregation events

Number of events by group size

event_counts_Tigers_NWI <- events_NWI[, .(Num_Events = .N), by = Max_N_Sharks][order(Max_N_Sharks)]

event_counts_Tigers_NWI

Event duration

Event duration is the time between the first and last detection in the event. An event in which every individual was detected only once within a few seconds therefore has a duration close to zero.

events_NWI[, Event_Length_Minutes :=
             as.numeric(difftime(Event_End_Time, Event_Start_Time, units = "mins"))]

Tigers_NWI_final <- merge(Tigers_NWI_final,
                          events_NWI[, .(Event_ID, Event_Length_Minutes)],
                          by = "Event_ID", all.x = TRUE)

events_NWI

Time each individual spent in each event

For each individual within each event: the time of its first and last detection, and the time between them (Residency_Minutes).

residency_time_NWI <- Tigers_NWI_final[, .(
  transmitter_id    = transmitter_id[1],
  First_Detection   = min(detection_datetime),
  Last_Detection    = max(detection_datetime),
  Residency_Minutes = as.numeric(difftime(max(detection_datetime), min(detection_datetime),
                                          units = "mins"))),
  by = .(Event_ID, transmitter_deployment_id, station_name)]

residency_time_NWI

Shortest period in which all individuals in an event were detected

An event lasting several hours may include only a brief period when all individuals were present together. For each event we find the shortest span of time containing at least one detection of every individual in that event. For example, if three sharks form an event, this is the shortest interval in which all three were detected.

The function works through the detections in time order. From each detection it moves forward until every individual has been seen, records the length of that span, and keeps the shortest span found.

min_window_all_individuals <- function(times, ids) {
  n_ind <- length(unique(ids))
  best  <- NA_real_
  for (s in seq_along(times)) {
    # Stop once the remaining detections can no longer include every individual
    if (length(unique(ids[s:length(ids)])) < n_ind) break
    seen <- c()
    for (e in s:length(times)) {
      seen <- union(seen, ids[e])
      if (length(seen) == n_ind) {
        span <- as.numeric(difftime(times[e], times[s], units = "mins"))
        if (is.na(best) || span < best) best <- span
        break
      }
    }
  }
  best
}

min_max_shark_window <- Tigers_NWI_final[order(detection_datetime), .(
  min_duration_mins = min_window_all_individuals(detection_datetime, transmitter_deployment_id)),
  by = Event_ID]

Tigers_NWI_final <- merge(Tigers_NWI_final, min_max_shark_window, by = "Event_ID", all.x = TRUE)
events_NWI       <- merge(events_NWI,       min_max_shark_window, by = "Event_ID", all.x = TRUE)

events_NWI

Plots

All detections at the focal receivers

An abacus plot of every detection at each focal receiver.

Abacus_Plot_Tigers_NWI <- ggplot(Tigers_NWI_dt,
                                 aes(x = detection_datetime, y = station_name)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8, colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "Receiver") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.title         = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
        axis.text          = element_text(size = 11),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor   = element_blank())

Abacus_Plot_Tigers_NWI

Aggregation events at the focal receivers

Each point is one aggregation event, plotted at its start time and coloured by the number of individuals involved. Events with three or more individuals are drawn larger.

Tigers_NWI_Graph <- ggplot(events_NWI,
                           aes(x = Event_Start_Time,
                               y = factor(station_name, levels = sort(focal_stations)),
                               colour = factor(Max_N_Sharks),
                               size   = Max_N_Sharks >= 3)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_y_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1", name = "No. of individuals") +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 2, `TRUE` = 4), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "Receiver") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.title       = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
        axis.text        = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
        legend.title     = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
        legend.text      = element_text(size = 11),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

Tigers_NWI_Graph
